a, COS-7 cells expressing NUP98A221TAG were labelled with live-cell dyes (SiR-tetrazine and JF646-tetrazine) following genetic code expansion of either bicyclo[6.1.0]nonyne-lysine (BCN) or non-reactive control t-butyloxycarbonyl-l-lysine (BOC). Scale bars, 10 μm. b, Immunofluorescence images confirm that endogenous importin-β remains localized at the nuclear envelope after NUP98 click–labelling with HD653. Scale bars, 10 μm. c, Hydrodynamic radius of purified enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) containing BCN at residue 39 and labelled either with HD653 or the established anisotropy dye Cy3B30,31, determined from TRFA measurements in solution. The measured radii agree well with wild-type EGFP, validating HD653 as a reliable probe for fluorescence anisotropy. Box plots display the median (centre line), interquartile range (box), and whiskers extending to data points within 1.5×IQR; individual points represent n = 4 independent replicates. d, Summary of TRFA parameters extracted for all labelled positions across the FG domains in live cells: steady-state anisotropy, fundamental anisotropy (r0), residual anisotropy (rp), local rotational correlation time (ρfast), and relative amplitude of the slow (segmental) component (βslow) as defined in Eqs. 5 and 6. Box plots display the median (centre line), mean (central square), interquartile range (box), and whiskers extending to data points within 1.5×IQR. Sample sizes and statistical analyses are as described in Fig. 1g. e, Representative anisotropy decay curves for residues 36, 100, 312, 387 and 482 measured in the NPC, in isolated FG chains in solution, and in freshly formed FG condensates.

a, Estimation of endogenous importin-β concentration at the nuclear pore by immunostaining with Alexa Fluor 488–labelled antibody, followed by titration with free Alexa Fluor 488 dye in solution (1 µM–1 mM). Importin-β remained detectable up to 100 µM dye but became obscured at 1 mM, suggesting that the effective local concentration at the NPC approaches the millimolar range. b-e, TRFA parameters of purified NUP98 FG domains co-phase-separated with increasing molar ratios of importin-β: (b) fitted slow-component timescale ρslow, (c) fundamental anisotropy r0, (d) residual anisotropy rp, (e) fitted local dye motion ρfast. f-j, Apparent segmental motion, quantified by the fitted slow-component timescale, across multiple labelled sites in NUP98 FG domains in the absence and presence of importin-β (1:1 molar ratio). Data represent mean ± s.d. from n = 3 independent replicates.

a, Snapshots from the end of coarse-grained MD simulations showing co-condensation of NUP98 FG domains with importin-β at varying molar ratios (NImp-β/NFG) and different FG–importin-β interaction strengths (\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β). Importin-β is shown in red and NUP98 FG chains in grey. b, Concentration profiles of FG chains along the simulation box. The ratio of importin-β to FG chains (NImp-β/NNUP98) is indicated in each panel. The symbols and error bars represent the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. The solid lines represent double error function fits to the concentration profiles26. c, d, Experimentally measured FG-domain concentrations in freshly formed NUP98 FG condensates co-phase-separated with different molar ratios of importin-β: (c) FG concentration in the dense phase and (d) in the dilute phase from fluorescence experiments. Data represent mean ± s.d. from n = 5 independent replicates. Notably, in the absence of importin-β, FG chains form nanoscale assemblies that persist in solution, leading to a slightly elevated apparent concentration in the dilute phase. e, MD-simulated FG-chain concentrations in the dense phase of co-condensates of NUP98 FG domains and importin-β as a function of molar ratio NImp-β/NNUP98, comparing different FG–importin-β interaction strengths. Symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. The grey shading indicates the experimentally measured dense-phase concentrations from (c) (mean ± s.d.), narrowing the range of possible FG–importin-β interactions in the model to 0.4 <\(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β < 0.5.

a, Concentration profiles of importin-β beads along the simulation box for different molar ratios of importin-β to NUP98 FG chains (NImp-β /NNUP98). The solid lines are double-error-function fits26. b, Phase diagram summarizing the concentrations of importin-β in the dilute (\({c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dilute}}}\)) and dense phases (\({c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dense}}}\)) as a function of FG–importin-β interaction strength \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β, obtained from the profiles in (a). c, The partition coefficient of importin-β (\({c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dense}}}/{c}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}^{{\rm{dilute}}}\)) plotted as a function of molar ratio NImp-β/NNUP98 for \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.4 and 0.42. The dashed lines are fits of \(a{e}^{\frac{b{N}_{{\rm{Imp}}-{\rm{\beta }}}}{{N}_{{\rm{NUP}}98}}}\) to the data points within the range 0.5 ≤ NImp-β/NNUP98 ≤ 1. Extrapolation to the infinitely dilute limit (i.e., NImp-β/NNUP98 → 0) yields partition coefficients of 16.5 ± 6 for \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.4 and 1120 ± 364 for \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42. Proteomics data estimate the partition coefficient of importin β1 inside NPCs to lie between 400 and 1300 (dark grey rectangle; see Supplementary Text). To account for possible strong crowding effects in the NPC, compared to the cytosol/nucleus, the uncertainty band is extended downward by an additional factor of ten (light grey rectangle). For simulations with very low importin-β copy numbers, larger numerical uncertainties are expected, accounting for the observed outlier. FG–importin-β interactions of \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42 capture the proteomics-derived partition coefficient and are consistent with the measured FG concentration (Extended Data Fig. 3e). For \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β ≥ 0.44, nearly all importin-β molecules in the system are absorbed into the condensate (Extended Data Fig. 4a), consistent with an extrapolated partition coefficient far above 1000 and thus outside the expected range. In a-c, the symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ.

a, Snapshot of a simulation containing a single importin-β molecule (red) embedded in an NUP98 FG condensate (grey) uniformly filling a cubic box of width 38σ. b, Simulation for multiple importin-β molecules partitioned into an FG condensate confined to a slab geometry (360σ × 90σ × 90σ). For mean-squared-displacement (MSD) analysis, the box was divided into nine bins of width 40σ along the x-axis (vertical black lines). c, MSD of the centre of mass of a single importin-β molecule, ⟨ΔR2(t)⟩, for different FG–importin-β interaction strengths \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β. d, Averaged MSD of multiple importin-β molecules located near the centre of the condensate slab (bin range −20σ < x < 20σ), measured at 4.8 × 105τ. The interaction strengths were \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42 and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5. MSD components along the x-axis (left), y-axis (middle) and z-axis (right) are shown. The black dashed lines in (c) and (d) indicate linear fits to the MSD curves: in (c), fits were applied for t > 6 × 103τ; in (d), fits were applied for t > 15 × 103τ.

a, Concentration of importin-β in the dense phase of NUP98 FG condensates. Symbols represent the importin-β concentration at the centre of the condensate slab, cImp-β (x = 0); the symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ (see Extended Data Fig. 4a). The solid lines show fits of the function \(a{e}^{b{\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{\rm{FG}}-{\rm{Imp}}{\beta }}}\) to data points within the range 0.42 ≤ \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β ≤ 0.5. b, Translational diffusion coefficients (D) of importin-β inside FG condensates, rescaled by the diffusion coefficient of a single importin-β in solution, D0 (see Supplementary Fig. 3). For molar ratios NImp-β/NNUP98 = 0.2 to 2, the symbols represent diffusion coefficients of importin-β molecules located in the centre bin of the condensate slab (see Extended Data Fig. 5b). Diffusion was averaged over the y- and z-directions, D = (Dy + Dz)/2, i.e., directions parallel to the condensate interfaces. The mean was calculated from n = 90 simulation snapshots (sampled every 5000 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. The error bars indicate s.e.m. across all importin-β molecules within the central bin. The solid lines show fits of \({a}^{{\prime} }{e}^{{b}^{{\prime} }{\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{\rm{FG}}-{\rm{Imp}}{\beta }}}\) to the data points within 0.42 ≤ \({\widetilde{{\epsilon }}}_{{\rm{FG}}-{\rm{Imp}}{\rm{\beta }}-{\rm{\beta }}}\le 0.5\). c, Estimated diffusion flux of importin-β across the NPC \({J}_{{\rm{Imp}}{\rm{\beta }}}=A{c}_{{\rm{Imp}}}^{{\rm{dense}}}\times {D}_{{\rm{Imp}}{\rm{\beta }}}\). The symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 45000 simulation snapshots (sampled and time-averaged every 10 τ) over the last 4.5 × 105 τ. For reference, we used D0 = 51 μm2/s as the translational diffusion coefficient of free importin-β in solution (see Supplementary Text). The NPC was approximated as a cylinder of radius RNPC = 0.05 μm, height HNPC = 0.1 μm and volume \({V}_{{\rm{NPC}}}=\pi {R}_{{\rm{NPC}}}^{2}{H}_{{\rm{NPC}}}\). A geometric prefactor \({V}_{{\rm{NPC}}}/{H}_{{\rm{NPC}}}^{2}\) rescales the condensate-derived flux to the NPC geometry, neglecting effects from non-uniform spatial distributions.

a, Autocorrelation functions of the bond vector \({\langle \vec{{b}_{i}}({t}_{0}+t)\cdot \vec{{b}_{i}}({t}_{0})\rangle }_{{t}_{0}}\) for NUP98 FG domain at residues 36, 67, 100, 136, 151, 221, 251, 283, 312, 338, 362, 387, 426, 458, 482. Here, \(\vec{{b}_{i}}\) is the unit bond vector connecting residue i to i + 1. The black dashed lines show exponential fits of the form aexp(-t/τfast) and a’exp(-t/τslow) to the early [0,10τ] and late [25τ,100τ] decay regimes, respectively, providing a coarse approximation of the multi-exponential polymer dynamics. Points represent data from four independent simulation runs. Single-chain simulations were run for 105τ; condensate and NPC simulations for 104τ. Residue coordinates of the NUP98 FG domain were sampled every τ. The interaction strengths were \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–Imp-β = 0.42 for NPC simulations, and \(\widetilde{{\epsilon }}\)FG–FG = 0.5 for single-chain and condensate simulations. b, Slow relaxation times, τslow, obtained from fits to the late-time decay of the bond-vector autocorrelation functions. c, Fast relaxation times, τfast, obtained from fits to the initial decay. The symbols denote mean values, and error bars indicate the s.e.m. across the four independent runs.

a, Predicted O-GlcNAc modification sites (blue) within the second FG domain of NUP98, annotated using the O-GlcNAc Database v2.092. b–c, Mass spectrometry analysis of (b) wild-type and (c) enzymatically O-GlcNAcylated NUP98 FG domains. Each O-GlcNAc modification produces a mass increase of +203.08 Da. The dominant peak in (c) corresponds to approximately 17 GlcNAc moieties per polypeptide chain. d, Time-lapse fluorescence images showing phase separation of purified enzymatically O-GlcNAcylated NUP98 FG domains at 10 μM in vitro; TRFA experiments used 25 µM to obtain condensates of comparable size to unglycosylated condensates. Scale bar, 10 μm. e, Coomassie-stained SDS-PAGE gel showing that glycosylated NUP98 FG domains migrate more slowly than wild-type due to their increased molecular mass. f, Comparison of apparent segmental motion across multiple labelled sites in live-cell NPCs versus in vitro condensates under the indicated conditions. Phase separation of O-GlcNAcylated FG domains with importin-β closely recapitulates the relative apparent segmental-motion trends observed in live-cell NPCs. Sample sizes and statistical analyses are as described in the corresponding source figures (Fig. 1g for NPCs; Figs. 2c,d and 4h,i for FG condensates).

Bottom row: the axially averaged FG-NUP concentration (excluding FG-NUP358) over the last 600 ns of simulation (colour scale: linear 0–50 mg/mL; >50 mg/mL shown as uniform dark red; bin size Δr = Δz = 3 nm). Simulations in (a-d) were run for 2.5 μs. e, Root-mean-square inter-residue distance (RE) of NUP98 FG chains in the NPC. The symbols and error bars indicate the mean and standard error, respectively, calculated from n = 400 simulation snapshots (19200 NUP98 chain configurations) over four independent blocks of 150 ns. #1521. PM: Hojbjerg still an option for Milan – January move possible thanks to €15m price tag

AC Milan are reportedly interested in making a move for Pierre-Emile Hojbjerg when the January mercato opens, it seems.

There have been suggestions about a move for Hojbjerg for some time, and Milan could attempt a move in January, especially if Christian Comotto departs on loan. The Dane, according to PianetaMilan, is still an option for January if another midfielder is to arrive.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Of course, Luka Modric’s likely retirement at the end of the season will give the Rossoneri time to think about his replacement, or even replacements, and Hojbjerg could be a new tool for Ruben Amorim.

His contract with Marseille runs until the summer of 2028, so his value is only dropping, especially as he gets older. So, a bid of €15 million could be enough to land him.

The Diavolo have already been successful when it comes to recruiting from Ligue 1, look at the example of Adrien Rabiot and whilst they’re not the same, there are similarities. For example, the Dane got nine goal contributions last season.

It’s hardly his attacking work that is tempting Milan, though. Instead, his experience and quality would be welcomed, as would his physicality and reading of the game. He’d be suitable in a two or three-man midfield and he’s a new profile for Amorim. It makes complete sense why the interest is there.

#1520. Lazio lose Tavares and Sutalo for at least three weeks as Juventus chase 11-point gap

Defenders Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo hurt their hamstrings at Napoli, leaving unbeaten Serie A leaders Lazio short in defence. The setback hits Gattuso's back line just as Juventus return from the break chasing the leaders.

Lazio’s defence has suffered a double blow. Nuno Tavares and Josip Sutalo were both injured in the 1-1 draw at Napoli. The timing is awkward for the leaders, who resume their league campaign against Lecce on 21 November.

Exact recovery times will only be set once all clinical tests are complete. The early estimate is about 20 days for each player, Sky Sport Italia reported. On that timeline, both miss the home game against Lecce and could return for the trip to Torino on 28 November.

Not every report is that hopeful. Football Italia reported that the pair should miss both the Lecce and Torino games. Under that scenario, they hope to be available again in the first week of December. The match against Atalanta on 6 December is also in doubt.

Tavares has been a real attacking outlet this season. He has one goal and four assists in 11 Serie A games. He also has a long record of muscle injuries. Sutalo has made eight league appearances since joining on loan from Ajax on 22 August.

Lazio must now turn to their alternatives. Alfonso Pedraza, who joined from Villarreal in the summer, is the leading option at left-back. He has played 322 minutes across the league and Coppa Italia. Diogo Leite and Doekhi are competing to replace Sutalo in the middle.

The stand-ins inherit a strong record. Lazio have scored 25 goals and conceded 9 so far. Keeping that defensive record with a reshuffled back line is now Gattuso’s task.

Juventus know Lazio’s quality first-hand. Gattuso’s side won 3-0 in Turin earlier this season. That result still weighs on the table. Five wins, three draws and three defeats make up the Juventus record from their opening games.

— S.S.Lazio (@OfficialSSLazio) November 8, 2026

Two missing defenders will not close the gap on their own. They do, however, give Juventus a window in which the leaders are weaker than usual. Any dropped points by Lazio over the coming rounds would only count if Juventus take care of their own fixtures.

Those fixtures follow Lazio’s closely. Como v Juventus is scheduled for Sunday 29 November at 20:45, the day after Lazio’s game against Torino. Further ahead, Lazio’s aim is to have both defenders fit for the Rome derby on 13 December.

#1519. Defender David Bates recalled by Scotland after almost eight-year absence

Published: 13:34 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 13:45 EST, 11 November 2026

David Bates has been rewarded for a strong start to life in Turkey by earning a recall to the Scotland squad almost eight years after his last appearance for the national team.

The 30-year-old centre-back has been added to Sebastien Pocognoli’s group after Luis Binks withdrew ahead of the Nations League matches against North Macedonia on Friday and Switzerland on Monday.

Bates currently plays for Amedspor and has started all 11 matches this season as his club have soared to third in the Turkish Super Lig.

The defender won all four of his caps under Alex McLeish while playing for Hamburg in the 2018/19 campaign. His last appearance for the national team was in a 2-0 win over San Marino in a Euro 2020 qualifier in March 2019, in what also turned out to be McLeish’s last game in charge.

Former Rangers player Bates joined Amedspor in the summer after spending four years in Belgium with Mechelen and then Standard Liege following his Aberdeen exit in 2022.

Brondby captain Binks is the second centre-back to drop out of the squad initially named by Pocognoli last week, after Swansea’s Stephen Welsh sustained an injury and had to be replaced by Los Angeles FC’s Ryan Porteous last weekend.

David Bates playing for Scotland against Albania back in 2018

Sebastian Pocognoli is keen to create a winning culture in the Scotland squad

The head coach is viewing this month’s double-header as crucial to his preparations for the Euro 2028 qualification campaign, which could begin in March if Scotland are not involved in Nations League play-offs.

'I think that these two games are, if we start the qualification in March, the last package of games that we have to use to be ready for the March camp,' Pocognoli said.

'If it’s not the case (that the Euro campaign starts in March), we can play friendly games which can be useful for June, so we have more time to prepare. And maybe, if we are really strong in the next two games, maybe we have play-off games. That’s the ambition.

'These can be useful also for the process of the qualification. But if the qualification starts (in March), we need to be ready. That’s why this camp for me is crucial in terms of demanding to the players, try to impress me and do everything to improve.

'I believe if we want to go to the Euros and be successful, we need to build this qualification feeling by winning games and to build the best winning culture possible.'

#1517. Iraola fumes at bungling fourth official for costing Liverpool a penalty

Andoni Iraola wanted to talk about his team and their need to improve but how could he concentrate on something so straightforward when he had seen something so bizarre?

It is important, first and foremost, to explain this is not painting a narrative about Liverpool being unfortunate. Far from it. Iraola hissed his dismay that Nottingham Forest had shown more intensity and been the better team for long periods in an entertaining 2-2 draw.

But the penalty that changed the contest? Iraola, his coaching staff, even the supporters behind the dugout had been left flabbergasted that the malfunctioning number board of fourth official Tim Robinson presented an avenue for Forest to exploit.

Iraola had tried to make a triple change, wanting to introduce Ryan Gravenberch, Kostas Tsimikas and Rio Ngumoha, but as Robinson pressed buttons to no avail and everyone in Red became frustrated, Forest substitute Liam Delap took a quick throw and the Liverpool house almost caved in.

Neco Williams, once of Liverpool, surged into the penalty area, Alisson Becker arrived a fraction too late after the defender got his shot away and took his old team-mate down. Morgan Gibbs-White exacerbated the damage when sending Alisson the wrong way and this was the last thing a manager wanting to make an impression on a big day needed to see but this was reality.

Alisson takes out Neco Williams and Forest have a penalty! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/fX2flY3Tob

Gibbs-White converts from the spot to restore Forest's lead! 🌳🎯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/jeoPiXPArw

“I cannot explain because I don’t have an explanation,” Iraola said. “I wanted to make those substitutions about three minutes before. I mean, it was two, three, four times the ball had gone out. I still don’t know the reason why we couldn’t make the subs.

“I think [the fourth official] was having some problems with the board or something. It [the penalty] wouldn’t have happened if I had made the sub. I asked. I had complained the previous time. The supporters were shouting and they were aware of the situation. But I don’t know what happened and I don’t know why they have given the penalty.”

"A professional fourth official cannot take three minutes." 😳Andoni Iraola was not happy with the time taken to get the substitutes' board ready.🎙️ @jules_breach | 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/fMfYOjQJPd

He did know, though, why Liverpool had needed to drag themselves off the deck again for the second week in a row. Iraola has shown in his opening weeks on Merseyside that he is not someone who seeks excuses.

“A lack of intensity hurt us,” Iraola said with obvious disdain and it was only down to a show of character in the second period that a slovenly first half did not enable Forest to win at Anfield for the third consecutive year, for all that the travelling fans thought it was “happening again!”

Forest, bruised after two defeats in four days to Leeds, looked like an Oliver Glasner side. They were aggressive and well organised, the only failing was that physically they could not see the job through, but the Austrian insisted that will change in due course.

Once Glasner is settled in and he gets his transfer business done – “definitely one, possibly two and probably three,” was his mischievous reply to how the window will unfold – Forest will be a formidable proposition, especially if the first 45 minutes are a barometer.

They had been knocking on the door before Dan Ndoye eventually broke the deadlock, sweeping a left-footed drive past Alisson after Igor Jesus had won a header from a long clearance. It was a simple goal, marginally onside, but it was absolutely deserved.

Ndoye gives Forest the lead at Anfield! 🌳🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ag0oZ7UjTm

“There were many positive aspects,” said Glasner. “It has been a three-game week; some players played. We are getting more and more fitness, that is just the foundation of how we want to play. It is just a point but it still feels a bit frustrating, so we have to stay humble.”

"I think we were very poor in the first half." 😤Andoni Iraola gives his assessment of Liverpool's performance against Nottingham Forest.🎙️ @jules_breach | 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/COZfhwkLeX

Neco Williams and James McAtee react to Nottingham Forest's draw at Anfield 🌳🎙️ @lynseyhipgrave1 | 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/BjX0p1yQ1m

"We started the game pretty bad today." 😬Alexander Isak gives his assessment of Liverpool's performance at Anfield.🎙️ @jules_breach | 📺 TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/3wD0hplmQ6

The playmaker added another goal and assist to his tally this afternoon.

20 - Morgan Gibbs-White has been directly involved in 20 goals in 2026 (15 goals, 5 assists), the joint-most of any Premier League player in all competitions (level with Haaland).His 13 goals in the Premier League in 2026 are also the most of any player.Decisive. pic.twitter.com/p1wQFwXvsI

Liverpool and Forest are both made to wait for their first Premier League wins of the season as the two sides play out a pulsating 2-2 draw at Anfield.

Full-time scenes at Anfield as Liverpool and Nottingham Forest share the points 🤝📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/WqOpfU38es

Sels calmly comes out to claim a deep cross to relieve the pressure on Forest. Munoz runs back to dispossess Delap and win a free kick, giving Liverpool another chance to launch the ball forward.

Glasner makes a very late double change as Hudson-Odoi and Dominguez replace McAtee and Igor Jesus.

There will be five minutes of added time. Liverpool continue their relentless search for a third goal, while Forest are holding on.

It’s wave after wave of Liverpool pressure. Forest are camped inside their own half. Igor Jesus and Delap are chasing every loose ball, but Forest are struggling to get out at the moment.

Munoz’s goal has provided another twist in this pulsating encounter. Isak wins a free kick in such dangerous territory and Szoboszlai steps up to take it. The Hungarian slams a venomous effort wide of the far post. Can either side find a late winner?

What an incredible finish! Wirtz threads a delightful pass through to Munoz. With his back to goal, the winger swivels and takes the ball on the outside of Murillo, before smashing a thunderous effort into the roof of the net, which brushes the crossbar on its way in.

Munoz, take a bow! 🤯👏📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/GD8IAdy2rJ

Igor Jesus does brilliantly to escape Nyoni, before he is pulled to the ground by Arajou, who is booked. It’s been an excellent defensive effort from Forest.

Iraola makes his final two alterations as Araujo and Nyoni replace Jacquet and Mac Allister.  Szoboszlai then swings such an inviting delivery into the penalty area, but Isak miscues his strike with his left foot.

Amid the chaos, Alisson was booked just before the penalty after appealing the decision and Iraola has ordered a triple change, taking off Kerkez, Frimpong and Gakpo for Tsimikas, Gravenberch and Ngumoha. This has seen Szoboszlai move out to right back.

Andoni Iraola is about to make his substitution and this is interesting because he had planned to introduce Rio Ngumoha, Kostas Tsimikas and Ryan Gravenberch 10 minutes ago but told them to sit down after Liverpool had equalised. Forest have put Liam Delap on, giving him his debut after completing his £45m move to the club.

The Forest captain sends Alisson the wrong way, powering a clinical penalty into the net. Gibbs-White demonstrates fantastic composure and Liverpool have it all to do again.

Gibbs-White converts from the spot to restore Forest's lead! 🌳🎯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/jeoPiXPArw

Delap showcases excellent initiative and takes a quick throw-in to send Williams through on goal. Alisson rushes out and catches Williams as he attempts to lob the goalkeeper. Williams crashes to the ground and the referee points to the spot. Alisson is furious. What a chance for Forest to restore their lead.

Alisson takes out Neco Williams and Forest have a penalty! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/fX2flY3Tob

This game is being played at a ferocious pace and Forest’s club-record signing Delap enters the action as he replaces Ndoye. Can the former Chelsea striker mark his debut with a much-needed goal?

That leveller has injected so much energy into Liverpool. Anfield believes again. Isak really needed that goal.

So much credit must go to Gakpo. The winger shrugs off Williams and fires a pinpoint cross towards the back post. Isak is there and converts from close range. We’re set up for such an intriguing finale. Liverpool have the momentum now.

Isak equalises for Liverpool at the Kop end! 🔴🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/qKFxq2AqaB

Wirtz’s frustrating afternoon is compounded as he picks up a booking after hauling Murillo to the ground. Iraola looks to be readying some substitutions.

There is a very strange feeling here: it’s almost a case of the home fans waiting for Nottingham Forest to score a second goal rather than anticipating that Liverpool will equalise. The early buzz in the atmosphere has gone and that is because the gaps everyone can see in the make up of the team remain. How Bradley Barcola will transform this situation?

Jacquet’s pass is intercepted and Ndoye is released on the counter. He’s guided out wide by Van Dijk but still squeezes in a brilliant cross. Gibbs-White was running up the pitch in support and slowed down, meaning no one was there to turn in Ndoye’s delivery.

Munoz is the next player to be booked after reacting angrily to a decision. Iraola has to consider making some changes soon.

Aina catches Munoz with a late challenge and he’s the second Forest player to go into the referee’s book.

You can already see in this second half that there is acres of space for Forest to exploit on the counter as Liverpool push for a leveller. Munoz then heads a point-blank header over the bar. Luckily for the Spaniard, the offside flag was up against Gakpo.

We are back for the second half here at Anfield. Can Liverpool find a route back into this game or can Forest hold onto the three points?

It’s a bizarre situation for Liverpool. They could easily be level or be 2-0 down. But they trial just 1-0 at half-time. Wirtz and Gakpo are looking lively, but Isak has struggled to influence the game.

Dan Ndoye scores his first goal in the Premier League in 377 days 🤯 pic.twitter.com/tjSiGoSPyW

Forest have a slender one-goal advantage at the break after a frantic first half at Anfield. Ndoye curled the visitors into a well-deserved lead after 24 minutes, before Wirtz had a goal ruled out for offside. The German was then sensationally denied by Sels’ diving save as he tipped Wirtz’s header over the bar. Alisson then replicated Sels’ heroics, parrying Igor Jesus’ strike against the woodwork to stop Forest from doubling their lead.

What a move and what a save! Murillo sprays an inch-perfect pass out to Aina, who chops inside of Munoz and fires a low cross into Igor Jesus. The Forest striker shoots first-time from inside the penalty area, but his effort is sensationally parried onto the bar by Alisson. That is a world-class stop from the Brazilian goalkeeper.

A world-class save from Alisson denies Forest a second! 🤯🧤📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/4NtzROILrU

Igor Jesus receives the game’s first yellow card after clipping Mac Allister with an unnecessary challenge.

Liverpool then fly forward again as Gakpo nutmegs Williams. His cross trickles through to Munoz at the back post. The ball is slightly behind Munoz and he leans back before shooting, causing his strike to narrowly sail over the bar.

There will be three minutes of added time to conclude this first half.

Liverpool are applying all the pressure at the end of this first half. At times, Forest have had every outfield player behind the ball.

Sels makes a superb save! Gakpo takes on his marker on the outside and fires in a cross which Wirtz meets. The attacker gets in between Schlager and Aina to win the header, but his effort is excellently tipped over the bar by Sels.

Out of nothing, Liverpool are level. McAtee attempts to play out from a deep position and his pass is intercepted by Wirtz. The ball breaks to Frimpong, who slips a clever pass to Wirtz. The German playmaker swivels and slides a low effort into the bottom corner. It’s a brilliant finish, but Frimpong was in an offside position before he provided the assist. VAR confirms this and Liverpool’s joy has been cut short. That is a huge let off for Forest, who need to be more careful with possession in deeper areas.

Following that Forest goal, there was a small flurry of Liverpool pressure, with Szoboszlai having a free kick punched away by Sels. Murillo is then very careless with the ball and is dispossessed. This allowed Mac Allister to play in Isak, but the striker is crowded out by multiple Forest defenders before he can get a shot away.

For the third season in a row, Nottingham Forest lead at Anfield. The goal had been coming, too. Liverpool were bright early but suddenly big gaps have started appearing and Forest are wily enough to exploit. There are lots of gripes around the stands about it being “too easy” and this knowledgeable crowd are right. A long ball forward and a simple flick has caused mayhem.

Forest are ahead and are well worth their lead. Sels launches a long ball up to Igor Jesus, who takes it down with an exquisite touch. The ball then breaks to Gibbs-White. The Forest captain plays in Ndoye and the winger curls a clinical effort into the far bottom corner to send the away support wild.

Ndoye gives Forest the lead at Anfield! 🌳🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ag0oZ7UjTm

Liverpool are struggling to find any space in and around Forest’s midfield and defence. Isak and Wirtz have been on the periphery as the time ticks over midway point of the first half.

Huge chance for Forest! McAtee drops deep and picks out Ndoye with a teasing cross. The forward meets the delivery and his header bounces wide. Upon the replays, there looks to have been a push on Frimpong by Ndoye. The referee’s whistle wasn’t sounded so it would have been interesting to see what would of happened if that chance had been converted.

It’s been a really frantic start to this game. Out of possession, Forest are retreating into a really rigid back five formation. Going forward, Aina and Williams are getting up the pitch at every opportunity.

Aina stands up an inviting cross to the back post for Ndoye, who heads it back into the danger zone. Igor Jesus latches onto it, but Jacquet makes a goal-saving tackle to block the striker’s close-range effort.

Sensational block from Jeremy Jacquet to deny Igor Jesus! 🤯📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/XuhO1GuE9F

Van Dijk clips a long ball over to the onrushing Isak as Liverpool look to burst forward on the counter. Isak races onto it and enters the penalty area, but he’s chased by Jair Cunha who matches the striker for pace. There’s a shoulder-to-shoulder, and the Forest defender bumps Isak off the ball, before Milenkovic comes back to mop up the danger.

Ndoye attempts to sprint in behind Liverpool’s defence. He’s chased by Jacquet and Ndoye can’t quite take the ball under his spell. That is an early warning sign for Liverpool.

The hosts then go up the other end as Mac Allister threads a delightful pass through to Gakpo. The Liverpool forward tries to swivel and shoot, but Williams tracks back and makes a crucial tackle.

Frimpong gets in behind Forest’s backline and attempts to pick out Gakpo with a cross aimed towards the back post. However, the ball bobbles and the Liverpool right back overhits his delivery.

A very intriguing team selected by Andoni Iraola and one that illustrates his confidence. It could be viewed as big call to drop Ryan Gravenberch and Rio Ngumoha but Victor Munoz and Alexis Mac Allister both made a difference when they were introduced at St James’s Park last Sunday and they warrant their inclusion. Munoz won’t be fit enough to play 90 minutes but it will be fascinating to watch him, particularly as Bradley Barcola will soon arrive to play in the same position on the left flank.

We are now under way at Anfield. Can Iraola mark his first competitive home game with a win or will Glasner get up and running with Forest?

A roaring rendition of You’ll Never Walk Alone has just boomed around Anfield. We will now observe a minute’s applause for Liverpool legend Kevin Keegan, who passed away at the age of 75 in July.

We’re talking about Liverpool Football Club here, right? I mean, we’re talking about the greatest football club in the world. However, Spurs’ signings of Savinho and Omar Marmoush, as well as Manchester City’s potentially big-money pursuit of Enzo Fernandez, means that any exit for the Dutchman looks extremely complicated.

Gakpo scored Liverpool’s first equaliser in their chaotic 2-2 draw with Newcastle United and starts today on the left wing.

Nottingham Forest have smashed their club-record transfer fee to sign Chelsea striker Liam Delap for £50m on a five-year deal, ending a lengthy pursuit by both the club and their head coach Oliver Glasner.

The Frenchman was absent from PSG’s squad on Friday evening as Luis Enrique’s side drew 2-2 with Lille in Ligue 1.

Barcola is yet another big-money addition to Liverpool’s forward line, following on from the signings of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Hugo Ekitike last summer.

Nottingham Forest: Sels, Jair Cunha, Milenkovic, Murillo, Aina, Schlager, McAtee, Williams, Ndoye, Gibbs-White, Igor Jesus.

Team news is IN! 🔴 #LIVNFO pic.twitter.com/3avoOQOPrM

Anfield will host its first Premier League match of the 2026-27 season.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest at Anfield.

This encounter pits two summer appointments – Andoni Iraola and Oliver Glasner – against each other as they both search for their first top-flight win at their new clubs.

In the opening Premier League game-week, Iraola’s Liverpool needed a last-gasp 99th-minute penalty from Dominik Szoboszlai to rescue an unconvincing 2-2 draw with Newcastle United at St. James’ Park. Meanwhile, Nottingham Forest have suffered back-to-back home defeats in four days against Leeds United without scoring (1-0 Premier League, 2-0 Carabao Cup).

Iraola has been handed the unenviable task of steering Liverpool back on track following a hugely disappointing campaign under Arne Slot, whose side’s defence of their Premier League ended in a meek fifth-place finish despite spending more than £400m in the previous summer.

The former Bournemouth boss must uncover how to get the best out of big-money recruits such as Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, Milos Kerkez and Jeremie Frimpong, and also tighten up Liverpool’s vulnerable midfield and defence. Given the pressure of the job and the club’s hectic schedule while balancing domestic and European football, it’s a tough ask. However, Liverpool have agreed a £120m deal for Paris St-Germain winger Bradley Barcola to bolster their attacking reinforcements, but the transfer hasn’t been finalised in time for today’s match.

Last season, Forest endured an equally tumultuous campaign, churning through a staggering four managers, before eventually stumbling to a 16th-place finish. Glasner has been hand-picked by owner Evangelos Marinakis to usher in an era of stability and success, after winning the FA Cup, Community Shield and Conference League in just over two years at Crystal Palace.

Both Marinakis and Glasner are extremely ambitious and demanding figures. You’d imagine a top-half finish would be considered the absolute minimum for Forest, while Glasner’s track record of winning trophies surely indicates that Marinakis is eyeing some silverware at the City Ground.

It’s a meeting of two managers who must deliver. Three points for either side would serve as a much-needed tonic to kickstart their seasons.

Kick-off is at 12:30, with team news coming shortly.

#1516. Thuram and Locatelli absences leave Juventus midfield thin for four games in 12 days

Khéphren Thuram and Manuel Locatelli will miss the rest of 2026 after knee surgery, leaving Spalletti short in midfield for a congested run of fixtures. Højbjerg has emerged as the name Juventus want to cover the gap in January.

Two senior midfielders will be missing as Juventus head into a congested run of fixtures. Thuram should be back with the group in January, and Locatelli only in the spring, Sport Mediaset reported. Both men are recovering from operations on the right knee.

Thuram underwent chondroplasty to treat patellar chondropathy. Dr Bertrand Sonnery-Cottet carried out the procedure at the Hôpital Privé Jean Mermoz in Lyon. Locatelli had his external meniscus sutured, also in Lyon, after spraining the knee against Milan. He was due to start rehabilitation the day after the operation.

Spalletti now has to rely on Douglas Luiz, Koopmeiners and new signing Pape Matar Sarr in the middle. The run opens with Venezia at 12:30 on 22 November. Omonia visit the Allianz Stadium at 21:00 on 26 November. The trip to Como follows at 20:45 on 29 November. The sequence closes with a Coppa Italia last-16 tie against Sassuolo.

Como present a sharp test. Fàbregas’s side have 23 points. They play a European fixture on 24 November, five days before they host Juventus.

The table leaves little room for slips. Juventus have 18 points from five wins, three draws and three defeats. They are 11 points behind leaders Lazio and six points off the Champions League places.

Sarr arrived on 1 September on loan from Tottenham until 30 June 2027. Juventus paid a €2.5 million fee plus €0.3 million in additional costs. The deal includes a €27.5 million permanent transfer, spread over three financial years. That becomes compulsory if certain conditions are met during 2026/27. The club describes him as a physically strong box-to-box midfielder. He has more than 100 Premier League appearances and won the 2024/25 Europa League with Spurs.

There is some relief elsewhere in the squad. Nico Gonzalez, Conceição and Cambiaso could all be available for Venezia. Yildiz hopes to return around December.

The absences make a January move for a midfielder more likely. Juventus have three targets for the window: a centre-forward, a defensive midfielder and a left-back. Pierre-Emile Højbjerg is the name for midfield, with Sørloth and Miranda also on the list, QS reported.

The profile is clear. Juventus want an experienced midfielder to bridge the gap until Thuram returns and Locatelli follows later. These remain media reports rather than a club statement.

Until then, the existing group must carry the load. The Coppa Italia tie with Sassuolo is set for the Allianz Stadium in Turin on Thursday 3 December at 21:00.

Published: 07:23 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 14:24 EST, 11 November 2026

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has revealed how passionate Prince William is about his beloved football club and opened up on their relationship.

The Prince of Wales, 44, has been a fan of Villa since his days at Eton when he idolised club legend Paul McGrath - shunning the more conventional Premier League big beasts supported by his schoolmates.

He regularly attends matches at Villa Park and across Europe alongside his son George, and he has been a prominent figure during their success under Emery in recent times.

This included the Prince partying with Villa's squad after last season's Europa League triumph and he watched them against Barcelona in the Champions League at the Nou Camp last week.

And, in a special edition of Country Life magazine, which was guest edited by the 44-year-old, Emery reflected on their relationship and how often they talk about the club.

’During the transfer window, he’s asking about the team every day,' the Villa boss said. 'How is the team? How are you? How are we going to play some players? How are we going to do? He is always so close to us and we appreciate it so, so much.

Unai Emery has revealed how passionate Prince William is about Aston Villa and opened up on their relationship

The Prince pictured alongside his son George at Villa's game against Barcelona last week

A special edition of Country Life, guest edited by the 44-year-old, featured a piece on Emery

’When he’s with us, he’s a fantastic guy. We’ve had lunch together, he’s watched training sessions, we share conversations, everything about football. He shows his humble personality with us - I can’t forget it. For me, it seems unbelievable.

'He’s our boss, but he’s always trying to be at our level, respecting so much everything we are doing here. If he’s sitting with us to have lunch, he asks “Where am I sitting?” Wherever you want! It’s fantastic.

‘We are scoring, he is celebrating, it is fantastic for us. If we can give him good news, good results, good moments in football, we are proud of it.’

In the same article, the Prince of Wales went on to reflect on his love of football and Villa, revealing how he has become increasingly passionate over the years.

He added: 'Football feels like a second family to me, I love the tribal nature of being among others who support the same team. We all experience the highs and lows of following that team together and you get the feeling that you belong somewhere.

'I used to be a defender, usually right back, and I’m hoping to play in a few fathers’ five-a-side matches. Since having children, I’ve become even more fanatical than I thought I would be about the game.

'I wasn’t like this when I was 18 or 20, I kept an eye from a distance. Now, I probably think and talk about Aston Villa every day. I enjoy looking to see what is going on: the stats, the players’ recovery, tactics and matches.'

The Prince is regularly pictured watching his beloved team at Villa Park and across Europe

When asked previously about why he settled on the Midlands club, Prince William shared that it was the thrill of supporting a club without season after season of successes which had brought him to Villa.

'A long time ago at school I got into football big time. I was looking around for clubs. All my friends were either Man United fans or Chelsea fans and I didn’t want to follow the run-of-the-mill teams,' he told the BBC in 2015.

'I wanted to have a team that was more mid-table that could give me more emotional rollercoaster moments.

'Aston Villa’s always had a great history. I have got friends of mine who support Aston Villa and one of the first FA Cup games I went to was Bolton v Aston Villa back in 2000. Sadly, Villa went on to lose to Chelsea (in the final).

'It was fantastic, I sat with all the fans with my red beanie on, and I was with all the Brummie fans and had a great time.

'It was the atmosphere, the camaraderie and I really felt that there was something I could connect with.'

#1513. Juventus and Torino the only Serie A sides without a penalty either way after 11 rounds

Eleven rounds into the Serie A season, Juventus have neither won nor conceded a penalty, a distinction shared only with Torino. With the league's penalty rate down and the team seventh, the João Mario handball in Florence has become the clearest example of a call that went against them.

Juventus have reached the November break without a single penalty decision in their league matches. Seven sides are still waiting for a penalty in their favour: Roma, Juventus, Torino, Lecce, Fiorentina, Sassuolo and Udinese. Seven have yet to concede one: Inter, Milan, Como, Juventus, Napoli, Torino and Genoa. Only the two Turin clubs appear on both lists.

That makes Juventus an outlier, even in a season of fewer spot-kicks. Sportmediaset puts the number of teams still waiting for a penalty partly down to the new refereeing approach introduced by Orsato.

The wider numbers show a quieter season from the spot. The 24 penalties so far work out at about 0.22 per match, compared with 0.28 and 0.27 in the two previous seasons. The drop was sharpest early on. Only five of the 24 penalties came in the first five rounds.

The trend has not been flat since then. The rate rose to 0.31 per match after the September international break. Juventus have not shared in that rise. Their total in both columns remains zero.

The contrast with last season is clear. Juventus were awarded five league penalties then. They also had the last three saved: David’s against Lecce, Yildiz’s against Cremonese and Locatelli’s against Sassuolo.

The case that has drawn most attention came late in the 2-2 draw at Fiorentina. João Mario handled the ball. No penalty was given. Gianluca Rocchi, who now works as a DAZN pundit, said it should have been a spot-kick. His reasoning was that the arm was out wide and the player had time to move it, even though the ball came from a teammate.

Luciano Spalletti signalled that he also saw a penalty. He chose not to complain publicly about the decision.

Close calls carry weight at this stage. Juventus are seventh on 18 points, six behind fourth place. Champions League qualification is in doubt. An injury-hit squad cannot easily absorb lost points from decisions at the margins.

The run after the break will test whether the pattern holds. Venezia, the next league opponents, are among five clubs to have conceded three penalties, the league’s highest total. Frosinone, Bologna, Atalanta and Sassuolo share that figure. Sassuolo are also on the list of sides yet to be awarded one.

The schedule is crowded. After Venezia, Juventus host Omonia in the Europa League. A league trip to Como follows, then Sassuolo at home in the Coppa Italia. Como have yet to concede a penalty this season.

The first of those fixtures has already moved. Lega Serie A brought Juventus v Venezia forward to Sunday 22 November at 12:30, from its original slot on Monday 23 November at 20:45.

#1512. I won't do a Mauricio Pochettino! Thomas Tuchel insists there is 'zero chance' he will walk out on England for a Premier League job - but admits he misses club football

Published: 14:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 15:19 EST, 11 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel will stay loyal to England until the end of his contract at the 2028 European Championship but admits that he does miss the regular thrill of club management.

As Mauricio Pochettino prepares to activate a release clause with the USA national team to take the Manchester United job, England boss Tuchel has vowed to ignore all outside offers until the end of his deal with England.

‘There is no release clause,’ said Tuchel. ‘I signed the contract. I want to stay until the Euros. I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.’

After that Tuchel said that he is open-minded.

Asked whether he could stay longer with England, he said with a smile that: ‘I am open to everything.’

The chances are, though, that England will be looking for a new coach once the 2028 Euros are done.

Thomas Tuchel has revealed he misses club football - but won't walk out on England

He enjoys the buzz of managing 50 matches per season but is contracted until 2028

‘I miss the 50 [club] matches a season,’ Tuchel said. ‘I miss those two minutes when everything is done. You go out the two minutes before the first whistle goes. It's like the best two minutes.

‘Everything is done. You're in a full stadium. Lights are on and you're just so excited and you're part of it.

‘That's actually the two minutes where I realise how lucky and how grateful I am. Then the whistle goes, and then you're just in the tunnel again, trying to win the game for your team.’

Tuchel originally signed a short-term deal through to last summer’s World Cup but extended it until the Euros in the months before the tournament that ended with a semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Asked if there was ‘zero chance’ of him leaving before the end of his contract, he said: ‘I would say so.

‘First of all, I'm very grateful for what I have here because I know how rare it is to be in love with your team and to have the trust and to be able to work freely with your coaching staff, which I am.

‘I love my group of players. I love my staff and I have bosses who trust me and are happy with the way we do things.

Pochettino is set to become the new manager of Manchester United, replacing Michael Carrick

‘So, it's a lot. And I know how to appreciate it a lot.

‘It's in a good place. I'm in a good place. I'm desperate to win the Nations League and to play and try to win the Euros.’

England face Croatia at Wembley tonight in the Nations League before heading to Madrid for their final group game against Spain on Sunday. If England win both matches, they will top their group ahead of next March’s quarter-finals. At the very least they should progress as a second placed team.

The four teams emerging from next spring’s quarters will play Nations League semi-finals and final in one country next summer. With a venue yet to be chosen by UEFA, the FA are expected to throw their hat into the ring as a prospective host.

Tuchel has spoken before about the struggles England sometimes have in taking training performances on to the pitch and agreed that hosting the Nations League latter stages could act as a decent warm up before the challenges of playing a big tournament in front of a home crowd a year later.

‘The Nations League helps in general for us and I think to have it here could be exciting,’ Tuchel said.

‘It would be nice to have it here. So first of all, we need to reach the final before we play.

‘Playing at home is a challenge. It should be a home advantage when we go to the Euros and it should not become a home disadvantage that we feel in our brain.

‘It should be exciting and that's why it's also important what we are building at the moment and how the team plays.’

#1511. Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Transcriptional addiction to the androgen receptor (AR) underlies metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer1, in which AR maintains oncogenic programs through domain-specific interactions with the acetyltransferases p300 and CBP (collectively p300/CBP)2. Here we describe a novel therapeutic modality, domain-alteration chimeras (DALTACs), that rewire endogenous protein complexes by enforcing non-native domain–domain interactions. Our first-in-class AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-1 induces synthetic proximity between the ligand-binding domain of AR and the bromodomain of p300/CBP, misconfiguring their native interface and locking the complex in a non-productive state. DALTAC-1 triggers a ‘super-inhibitory’ effect, suppressing AR-driven transcription and proliferation more potently than combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition. Mechanistically, DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate engagement, abolishing the histone mark H2B N-terminal acetylation and inducing neomorphic acetylation of AR and coactivators, ultimately collapsing the AR neo-enhanceosome. Chromatin profiling revealed redistribution of AR and p300/CBP towards palindromic androgen response elements, accompanied by disruption of cofactor and transcriptional machinery recruitment at oncogenic AR and ERG neo-enhancers. DALTAC-1 exhibits exquisite lineage selectivity, displaying potent activity in AR–p300/CBP dual-dependent cells and sparing AR-negative cells. In multiple in vivo models, DALTAC-1 induces deep and durable tumour regressions. Together, these findings establish DALTACs as a broadly applicable strategy to rewire disease-defining complexes through domain-topology alteration, expanding induced-proximity therapies, and the precise lineage selectivity of DALTAC-1 supports its translational potential in AR-driven prostate cancer.

Aberrant enhancer-driven transcription sustains many cancers, including metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC)3,4. AR, a central driver of mCRPC, undergoes ligand-induced activation and dimerization upon binding to androgen response element (ARE)-enriched enhancers and assembling cancer-specific neo-enhanceosomes4,5,6. These complexes depend on the paralogous acetyltransferases p300 and CBP7. p300 has been identified as the predominant paralogue supporting AR-positive (AR+) prostate cancer growth, and the p300/CBP-dependent enhancer mark H2B N-terminal acetylation (H2BNTac) and AR–p300 co-bound enhancer activity are increased in prostate tumours8. Previous studies showed that the N-terminal domain (NTD) of AR interacts with p3002, and this interaction stimulates the histone acetyltransferase (HAT) activity of p300, leading to enhancer remodelling and transcriptional activation by establishing a permissive chromatin environment9,10. Although p300/CBP-targeted therapies have been developed for castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC)11,12, global p300/CBP inhibition may cause toxicity in normal tissues13.

Chemically induced proximity (CIP) reprograms protein–protein interactions to manipulate cellular functions14,15. Established CIP modalities include proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), which promote target protein degradation via E3 ligase recruitment16; regulated induced proximity targeting chimeras (RIPTACs), which couple disease-associated proteins to essential effectors17,18; transcriptional/epigenetic chemical inducers of proximity (TCIPs), which redirect transcriptional coactivators19,20,21; and targeted relocalization activating molecules (TRAMs), which alter protein localization22. These approaches predominantly connect non-native partners. Here we introduce DALTACs, which enforce neomorphic domain interactions between physiological partners to disable endogenous oncogenic complexes. DALTAC-1 (JZY3032) connects the ligand-binding domain (LBD) of AR to the bromodomain (BRD) of p300/CBP, reprogramming substrate engagement, eliminating H2BNTac and suppressing AR–p300/CBP-dependent transcription. DALTAC-1 outperforms combined AR and p300/CBP inhibition, selectively targets AR-dependent prostate cancer, and induces tumour regression without overt toxicity, establishing domain-level rewiring as a promising therapeutic strategy.

Previous studies established that AR physically interacts with the coactivator p300 through its NTD2, and that dimerized transcription factors can stimulate p300 HAT activity9. To reprogram this native interaction, we designed heterobifunctional molecules that tether an AR-LBD binder to a p300/CBP-BRD binder through an appropriate linker. We reasoned that these molecules would induce non-native AR–p300/CBP interactions and thereby inhibit the growth of AR+ cancer cells by concurrently inhibiting both AR and p300/CBP functions (Fig. 1a).

To test this premise, we designed and synthesized a series of heterobifunctional molecules using a potent p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor (GNE-04912) and a selective AR-LBD binder23 tethered through a linker (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We selected the tethering site in the p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor based upon the co-crystal structure with GNE-049 and its analogues, which showed that our selected tethering site was exposed to the solvent environment24. Similarly, we chose the tethering site in the AR binder on the basis of our modelled complex structure with AR and extensive structure–activity relationships reported for this class of AR inhibitors23,25. We evaluated our synthesized compounds with proliferation assays in AR+ LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, which were shown to be responsive to p300/CBP-BRD inhibitors and PROTAC degraders11,26. GNE-049, the AR binder JZY3221, and their combination were included as controls. Treatment with GNE-049, JZY3221 or their combination showed limited inhibitory activity, particularly in 22Rv1 cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

To optimize these heterobifunctional molecules, we replaced the tetrahydropyran group of GNE-049 with a piperidinyl group that preserves p300 binding24 and systematically varied linker composition, length and rigidity (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Supplementary Note 1). Several compounds showed substantially greater anti-proliferative activity than the parent-inhibitor combination. Compound 7 (JZY3031) emerged as a lead, with half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) values of 1.9 nM and 2.6 nM in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, respectively, and was more potent than the inhibitor combination (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

Replacing an oxygen atom in the AR-binding moiety of compound 7 with an N-methyl group, a modification previously shown to improve oral bioavailability25, generated JZY3032 (Fig. 1b). JZY3032 achieved IC50 values of 0.26 nM and 1.0 nM in LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, respectively, and was more potent than the parent-inhibitor combination (Extended Data Fig. 1b). JZY3032 also showed improved systemic exposure and 18.5% oral bioavailability in mice, despite its high molecular mass of 975 Da (Extended Data Fig. 1c).

In an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) measuring induced AR–p300 complex formation, compound 7 and JZY3032 were the most potent and effective compounds that we tested. JZY3032 also produced the strongest inhibition of AR transcriptional activity in HEK293 ARE–GFP reporter cells (Extended Data Fig. 1b). By contrast, three enzalutamide-based bifunctional molecules were substantially less active in VCaP, LNCaP and 22Rv1 cells, demonstrating the importance of the AR-binding moiety (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e).

Based on its cellular, biochemical and pharmacokinetic properties, we designated JZY3032 as DALTAC-1. We also generated Neg-1, with reduced p300/CBP binding24, and Neg-2, with reduced AR binding27 (Extended Data Fig. 1f). Fluorescence polarization assays confirmed their intended binding profiles (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i). Cellular thermal shift assays further showed that DALTAC-1 stabilized AR, p300 and CBP, but not BRD4, supporting selective engagement of its intended targets (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1j).

To assess the activity and selectivity of DALTAC-1, we compared its anti-proliferative activity with the p300/CBP dual degrader CBPD-4098 and the combined treatment with the p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor GNE-049 (p300/CBPi) and AR-LBD binder JZY3221 (ARi). DALTAC-1 potently inhibited growth across all tested AR+ prostate cancer cell lines, with activity comparable or superior to CBPD-409 and consistently greater than p300/CBPi plus ARi in CellTiter-Glo (CTG) and colony-formation assays (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). This superiority suggests a gain-of-function mechanism arising from enforced miswiring of AR–p300 domain interactions. DALTAC-1 also retained potent activity in the AR-V7-high, p300/CBP-dependent 22Rv1 and CWR-R1 models (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b) and outperformed enzalutamide, darolutamide28,29, the AR PROTAC degrader ARV-76630 and the recently reported AR–BRD4 RIPTAC-131 (Extended Data Fig. 2c). By contrast, the inactive analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 showed substantially reduced activity, and excess p300/CBPi or ARi competitively attenuated DALTAC-1 activity, demonstrating that engagement of both targets is required (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e).

Compared with CBPD-409, DALTAC-1 exhibited markedly reduced cytotoxicity in AR-negative yet p300-dependent Kelly and NCI-H211 cells8 (Extended Data Fig. 2f). It remained highly active in AR+ MDA-MB-453 cells32, which depend on both AR and p300/CBP, but showed minimal activity in AR+ U-87 MG cells33, which were less sensitive to CBPD-409 and ARV-766 (Extended Data Fig. 2g). Across a broader cancer cell line panel, CBPD-409 displayed activity across multiple lineages, whereas DALTAC-1 selectively inhibited AR+ prostate cancer cells (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 2h). Moreover, a 4-h DALTAC-1 pulse followed by washout produced inhibition comparable to continuous exposure, whereas CBPD-409 or p300/CBPi plus ARi activity was substantially diminished after washout (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j). Collectively, these findings establish DALTAC-1 as a potent, durable and lineage-selective heterobifunctional compound whose activity depends on dual AR and p300/CBP engagement.

Ternary complex formation is central to the CIP strategy34. Using purified proteins, DALTAC-1 induced AR–p300 association in a concentration-dependent manner, whereas the combined AR and p300/CBP inhibitors and the binding-deficient analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 did not induce association (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) further demonstrated DALTAC-1-dependent complex formation. In the presence of 10 μM DALTAC-1, titration of GST–AR-LBD produced concentration-dependent binding to p300, with an apparent dissociation constant (Kd) of 333.1 nM, whereas minimal interaction between GST–AR-LBD and p300 was detected under the DMSO control condition (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Reciprocally, titration of DALTAC-1 at a fixed GST–AR-LBD concentration (1 μM) progressively increased the binding response, yielding an apparent Kd of approximately 4.3 μM (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Neither DALTAC-1, GST–AR-LBD, nor their combination produced significant binding to immobilized Flag–FOXA1 (residues 1–268), excluding nonspecific association with the immobilized protein or sensor (Extended Data Fig. 3d). Moreover, the individual AR-LBD and p300/CBP-BRD inhibitors, alone or combined, did not induce complex formation, whereas excess p300/CBP-BRD inhibitor markedly attenuated the DALTAC-1-induced BLI signal (Extended Data Fig. 3e,f). Together, these results demonstrate that DALTAC-1 specifically recruits the AR-LBD to p300 to promote concentration-dependent formation of the AR-LBD–DALTAC-1–p300 ternary complex.

Intracellular ternary complex formation was confirmed by ELISA, which showed that DALTAC-1, but not Neg-1 or Neg-2, enhanced AR–p300 association in VCaP cells (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Co-immunoprecipitation similarly demonstrated that DALTAC-1 enhanced the interaction between AR and p300/CBP (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i). Consistently, reciprocal immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry analyses identified AR as strongly enriched in p300 immunoprecipitates, and p300/CBP were among the most enriched AR-associated proteins following DALTAC-1 treatment (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3j,k). Proximity ligation assays (PLAs) further showed DALTAC-1 increased AR–p300 proximity, which was competitively blocked by either p300/CBPi or ARi (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m). Sequential co-immunoprecipitation of co-expressed Flag–AR, haemagglutinin (HA)–AR, and V5-p300 showed that DALTAC-1 maintained the interaction of HA–AR with Flag–AR from p300-containing complexes, indicating the incorporation of multiple AR molecules into the DALTAC-1-induced complex and supporting AR dimerization within the complex (Extended Data Fig. 3n). In 22Rv1 cells, DALTAC-1 enhanced p300 association with full-length AR but not the LBD-deficient AR-V7 variant, demonstrating the LBD dependence of the association (Extended Data Fig. 3o). DALTAC-1 also promoted p300 association with the DNA-binding-deficient AR-C619Y mutant35 (Extended Data Fig. 3p), indicating that complex formation does not require AR binding to DNA. Together, these findings demonstrate that DALTAC-1 induces the formation of a LBD-dependent AR–p300 complex.

Domain-resolved interaction mapping in HEK293 cells showed minimal basal association between AR and the p300 core region, comprising the BRD, RING/PHD and HAT domains, yet DALTAC-1 strongly enhanced this interaction (Extended Data Fig. 3q). Reciprocal domain mapping demonstrated that DALTAC-1 selectively recruited the AR-LBD, but not the AR-NTD, to p300 (Extended Data Fig. 3r). Accordingly, co-expressed AR-LBD and p300 core region showed minimal basal association but robust complex formation following DALTAC-1 treatment (Extended Data Fig. 3s), establishing a non-native AR-LBD–p300 core interaction.

To investigate its structural basis, we modelled the AR-LBD–DALTAC-1–p300-BRD ternary complex and the corresponding binary complexes, followed by 1-µs molecular dynamics simulations. The top-scoring ternary model predicted an AR–p300 interface stabilized by polar and hydrophobic interactions (Extended Data Fig. 3t). Key contacts included salt bridges between Asp1088 of p300 and Arg871 of AR and between Arg1133 of p300 and Glu872 of AR; hydrogen bonds involving AR Arg871–p300 Gly1085 and AR Ile816–p300 Leu1083; hydrophobic packing between Ile816 of AR and Leu1083 of p300; and a cation–π interaction between His874 of AR and the piperazine moiety of DALTAC-1. Molecular mechanics-generalized born surface area (MM-GBSA) analysis yielded a more favourable model-dependent interaction-energy estimate for the ternary complex (−161.8 ± 0.6 kcal mol−1) than for the DALTAC-1–AR (−81.4 ± 0.6 kcal mol−1) or DALTAC-1–p300 (−90.3 ± 0.4 kcal mol−1) binary complexes (Extended Data Fig. 3u,v). Computational removal of DALTAC−1 yielded an AR–p300 interface energy of −53.5 ± 1.1 kcal mol−1, consistent with favourable protein complementarity (Extended Data Fig. 3v).

Experimentally, mutation of the predicted interface residues in AR(R871A/E872A) and p300(D1088A/R1133A) substantially impaired DALTAC-1-induced complex formation (Extended Data Fig. 3w). Together, these findings establish that DALTAC-1 rewires AR–p300 domain interactions to form a stable ternary complex, providing a mechanistic basis for its downstream epigenetic and transcriptional effects.

In contrast to the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409, DALTAC-1 did not reduce p300/CBP protein abundance but rapidly suppressed H3K27ac and H2BK20ac, two histone marks associated with active enhancers (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). H2BNTac is deposited exclusively by p300/CBP and marks active enhancers in prostate cancer8. Our data demonstrate that DALTAC-1 exerts a de novo heterobifunctional effect by potently suppressing this critical histone mark without degrading p300/CBP. This level of H2BNTac suppression was not observed with the inactive analogues Neg-1 and Neg-2 or with the combination of AR and p300/CBP inhibitors (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c). DALTAC-1 also showed limited activity in AR-negative Kelly cells, supporting its AR-dependent selectivity (Extended Data Fig. 4d). Furthermore, in HEK293 cells, DALTAC-1-driven loss of H2BNTac increased in direct proportion to the amount of ectopically expressed AR, underscoring that both AR and p300 are required for DALTAC activity (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Moreover, a 2-h DALTAC-1 pulse caused sustained suppression of histone acetylation and MYC expression after washout, whereas the effects of combined AR and p300/CBP inhibitors were markedly reduced (Extended Data Fig. 4f).

Beyond histone substrates, p300/CBP acetylate non-histone regulators of transcription and signal transduction36. Whereas p300/CBP HAT inhibitors and degraders broadly suppress histone and non-histone acetylation7,8, acetyl-lysine profiling in VCaP cells revealed a distinct acetylation signature induced by DALTAC-1. DALTAC-1 strongly suppressed global histone acetylation, particularly enhancer-associated H2BNTac, more potently than combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4g–i). Consistently, immunoprecipitation–mass spectrometry identified H2B as the most significantly displaced p300 interactor, indicating disruption of p300 engagement with its canonical histone substrate (Extended Data Fig. 3j).

Concurrently, DALTAC-1, but not combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition, increased acetylation of AR and its cofactors SRC2 and SRC337 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4g,h,j,k). AR acetylation occurred in the NTD, suggesting that DALTAC-1-induced ternary complex formation redirects p300 catalytic activity towards the N terminus of AR as well as its associated cofactors. In an ARE reporter assay, glutamine substitution of the five SRC2 lysines most strongly acetylated by DALTAC-1 (multi-K-Q) modestly increased AR activity relative to wild-type SRC2, whereas alanine substitution (multi-K-A) modestly reduced it, indicating that acetylation at these sites has limited effects on SRC2 coactivator function (Extended Data Fig. 4l,m). Thus, DALTAC-1 suppresses enhancer-linked histone acetylation while selectively increasing acetylation of AR and its associated cofactors.

We next examined how DALTAC-1-mediated reprogramming of p300 substrate engagement affects transcription. DALTAC-1 strongly suppressed AR activity in an ARE–GFP reporter assay and repressed canonical AR target genes, whereas Neg-1, Neg-2 or combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition exhibited weaker effects (Extended Data Fig. 5a–c). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) in VCaP cells revealed downregulation of androgen response, p300/CBP target, MYC target and MTORC1 signalling pathways (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 5d–f). Chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) further showed rapid RNA polymerase II (Pol II) displacement from AR and p300 target loci (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Together, unlike the transcriptional activation mechanism of TCIPs19,20, DALTAC-1 represses AR–p300/CBP-driven oncogenic transcription.

Consistently, DALTAC-1 and the p300/CBP degrader CBPD-409 markedly reduced prostate-specific antigen (PSA), CCND1 and NKX3-1 protein levels, whereas combined p300/CBP and AR inhibition had modest effects on these proteins (Fig. 2g). Quantitative proteomics confirmed selective depletion of AR- and MYC-regulated proteins without reducing AR or p300/CBP abundance (Extended Data Fig. 5h). Together, these results show that DALTAC-1 reprograms p300/CBP substrate utilization to broadly suppress AR-driven oncogenic transcription.

We next tested whether this activity requires an antagonist-derived AR binder. We replaced the AR moiety of DALTAC-1 with enobosarm38, a non-steroidal AR agonist, to generate JZY4055 (Extended Data Fig. 5i). JZY4055 potently inhibited growth of AR+ VCaP cells (Extended Data Fig. 5j). Whereas enobosarm activated canonical AR target genes, JZY4055 repressed these genes and reduced p300/CBP-dependent H2BK20ac and H3K27ac, as well as the expression of AR- and p300/CBP-regulated proteins NKX3-1 and MYC (Extended Data Fig. 5k,l). These data demonstrate that AR–p300/CBP DALTAC-mediated transcriptional repression does not require an antagonist-derived AR binder.

p300/CBP are central AR coactivators that sustain oncogenic transcription through enhancer-associated histone acetylation8. To investigate how DALTAC-1 modulates p300 chromatin occupancy, we performed p300 ChIP–seq in VCaP cells. DALTAC-1 markedly expanded and redistributed p300 binding genome-wide (Fig. 3a). Approximately 40% of DALTAC-1-depleted peaks were promoter-proximal, whereas gained peaks occurred predominantly in intronic and distal intergenic regions, with only approximately 10% being located near promoters, indicating increased enhancer engagement (Fig. 3b). At AR-binding enhancer sites identified under DMSO (control) conditions, DALTAC-1 proportionally increased AR and p300/CBP occupancy (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 6a,b). Motif analysis revealed that gained p300 and CBP peaks were strongly enriched for canonical palindromic AREs and closely related nuclear receptor motifs, including progesterone- and glucocorticoid-response elements (PRE and GRE)39 (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). These findings demonstrate that DALTAC-1 redistributes p300/CBP through AR-dependent recruitment and stabilizes neomorphic AR–p300/CBP complexes on enhancer chromatin.

DALTAC-1 also significantly reshaped the AR cistrome (Fig. 3e). DALTAC-1 treatment increased AR occupancy at palindromic AREs while reducing binding at FOXA1–AR chimeric motifs associated with oncogenic AR neo-enhanceosomes40 (Fig. 3e,f and Extended Data Fig. 6e–g). Thus, rather than uniformly increasing AR binding, DALTAC-1 redirected AR away from oncogenic enhancers and concentrated it at canonical nuclear receptor response elements. Because AREs share substantial sequence similarity with PREs39, we examined whether their enrichment reflected progesterone receptor (PR) activation. DALTAC-1 instead reduced PR occupancy genome-wide while increasing AR occupancy at PR-binding sites (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i), indicating that these shared motifs were predominantly engaged by AR. Despite increased AR and p300/CBP binding, DALTAC-1 markedly decreased coactivator (BRD4 and ERG) recruitment, Pol II loading, and histone acetylation (H3K27ac and H2BK20ac) at AR/p300 co-bound enhancers (Extended Data Fig. 6j,k). DALTAC-1 therefore stabilized AR–p300/CBP chromatin binding while functionally decommissioning the associated transcriptional complexes.

Oncogenic transcription factors such as ERG and FOXA1 mutants are known to redirect AR to non-canonical AREs, thereby forming cancer-specific AR neo-enhanceosomes that drive lineage-dependent oncogene programs8,41. In TMPRSS2–ERG fusion-positive VCaP cells42, DALTAC-1 globally reduced ERG occupancy, although a subset of new ERG peaks emerged in intronic and distal intergenic regions (Extended Data Fig. 7a–d). Motif analysis revealed that DALTAC-1 depleted ERG binding at canonical ETS motifs and redistributed ERG towards palindromic AREs (Extended Data Fig. 7e). At non-promoter AR–ERG co-bound regions, DALTAC-1 increased AR and p300 occupancy, modestly increased SRC2 binding, and minimally altered FOXA1 occupancy (Extended Data Fig. 7f–h). Nonetheless, ERG and BRD4 binding declined, whereas Pol II occupancy and enhancer-associated histone acetylation were almost completely lost (Extended Data Fig. 7i). Thus, DALTAC-1 collapses AR–ERG neo-enhancers into a transcriptionally inactive state despite increased AR–p300 occupancy, dismantling the oncogenic output of the AR–ERG neo-enhanceosome (Fig. 3g and Extended Data Fig. 7j).

To assess DALTAC-1 efficacy across prostate cancer subtypes, we tested organoids derived from genetically engineered mouse models. We treated organoids derived from wild-type, Rosa26ERG/Pten−/−, Pten−/−, FOXA1 R265–71del+/+/Trp53−/− and Trp53−/− mouse prostates with DALTAC-141,43. DALTAC-1 preferentially reduced the number and size of Rosa26ERG/Pten−/− and FOXA1 R265–71del+/+/Trp53−/− organoids and suppressed MYC and CCND1 relative to wild-type, Pten−/− and Trp53−/− organoids (Extended Data Fig. 8a–d). Given that ERG and mutant FOXA1 enhance AR activity and sustain the AR neo-enhanceosome5,41,43,44, these findings suggest that DALTAC-1 effectively suppresses AR-driven prostate cancer. Furthermore, we evaluated DALTAC-1 efficacy across organoids derived from patient-derived xenograft (PDX) tumours45,46. Consistently, DALTAC-1 potently inhibited AR+ organoids, particularly AR+/ERG+ models (Fig. 4a). Thus, DALTAC-1 exhibits potent, lineage-selective activity across mouse and human organoid models.
